growth_story.headline: Singapore's growth slowed from 5.1 to 2.9 percent a year after 1997, with deep falls in world downturns; in 2025 income per person hit a new high.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 1997 Singapore's income per person grew 5.1 percent a year. From 1998 the pace settled at 2.9 percent a year, in an era marked by sharp falls during the Asian crisis in 1998, the dotcom crash in 2001 and the recession of 2008 and 2009. Recoveries followed, and the IMF judged the one after 2009, when income per person rose 12.5 percent in 2010, more vigorous than those after 2001 and 1998. Growth averaged 3.0 percent a year over 2006–2015 and 2.5 percent over 2016–2025, with swings tied to the global electronics cycle and, most recently, to demand for chips used in artificial intelligence. In 2025 income per person reached its highest level yet.

threads.title: Hit hard by world shocks
threads.text: Income per person fell 5.5 percent in 1998, 3.7 percent in 2001, and 3.4 and 2.8 percent in 2008 and 2009, years of the Asian crisis, the dotcom crash and a deep recession. The IMF found the 2008–09 recession less deep than feared, and the recovery after it more vigorous than those after the dotcom crash and the Asian crisis.

threads.title: Riding the electronics cycle
threads.text: Singapore's large electronics industry ties its growth to the global electronics cycle. After the Asian crisis it gained from a global electronics boom, and in 2023 a downturn in that cycle shrank manufacturing and slowed growth.

threads.title: AI chip demand lifts growth
threads.text: Global spending on artificial intelligence has raised demand for semiconductors, and this has supported Singapore's growth. In July 2026 the IMF credited AI-related chip demand, wage growth and public building works, and in December 2025 the Asian Development Bank pointed to strong global investment in AI and more infrastructure spending when it raised its outlook for Singapore.

threads.title: An ageing population
threads.text: Singapore's population is ageing fast. The IMF notes rising health care costs from ageing, and the government's Forward Singapore plan is framed around ageing and new technology, including artificial intelligence.

since_last_year.text: In May 2025 the IMF expected growth to slow because of trade tensions. Growth turned out stronger: income per person grew 3.7 percent in 2025, a little faster than the 3.3 percent of 2024. The IMF's July 2026 review credits demand for AI-related chips, wage growth and public building works. It also points to an energy shock from war in the Middle East, and lists a possible correction in AI-related investment among the risks.

growth_story.tension: The IMF reports that the economy still grew in 2023, despite the electronics downturn, and that foreign workers flowed in that year. Yet income per person fell 3.4 percent: the population grew faster than output. A year the sources call a slowdown shows up in the data as a fall.
